find: For OCR context questions, always connect Victorian social pressures to Stevenson’s methods.
replace: When you bring in context, always connect Victorian social pressures to Stevenson’s methods.
note: F3: OCR sets one extended response on the novella, not a separate context question.

find: The door on Bye Street
replace: The door on the by-street
note: F4: Stevenson never names the street; it is “a by-street”, a side street, not ‘Bye Street’.

find: sets out to hunt him by the door on Bye Street.
replace: sets out to hunt him by the door on the by-street.
note: F4: Stevenson never names the street; it is “a by-street”, a side street, not ‘Bye Street’.

find: Utterson says: “God bless me, the man seems hardly human! Something troglodytic, shall we say?… he gives a strong feeling of deformity, although I couldn’t specify the point.”
replace: Utterson says: “God bless me, the man seems hardly human! Something troglodytic, shall we say?” Enfield had already said in Chapter 1 that Hyde “gives a strong feeling of deformity, although I couldn’t specify the point.”
note: F5: ‘a strong feeling of deformity’ is Enfield in ch. 1, not Utterson in ch. 2; the two speeches were spliced into one.

find: Enfield tells the story of a “small man” who “trampled calmly” over a young girl and gave him “a look so ugly it brought out the sweat on me like running.”
replace: Enfield tells the story of a “little man” who “trampled calmly” over a young girl and then “gave me one look, so ugly that it brought out the sweat on me like running.”
note: F6: ch. 1 reads ‘a little man’ and ‘gave me one look, so ugly that it brought out the sweat on me like running’.

find: Carew is an “aged” gentleman with “silvery hair” — the symbol of Victorian respectability.
replace: Carew is “an aged beautiful gentleman with white hair” — the symbol of Victorian respectability.
note: F7: ch. 4 says ‘white hair’. ‘Silvery-haired’ belongs to the old woman at Hyde’s Soho house in ch. 4.

find: A servant girl watches from a moonlit window as Carew is “trampled” and “clubbed… with ape-like fury” by Hyde.
replace: A maid watches from a moonlit window as Hyde “clubbed him to the earth” and then, “with ape-like fury”, went on “trampling his victim under foot”.
note: F8: in ch. 4 Hyde clubs Carew down first; ‘ape-like fury’ belongs to the trampling that follows. The spliced quotation does not exist.

find: Stevenson puns on Utterson’s name (“he will be Mr Seek”) and on Hyde’s (“to hide”).
replace: Stevenson gives Utterson a pun on Hyde’s name: “If he be Mr Hyde… I shall be Mr Seek.”
note: F9: the pun is on Hyde/hide, and the ch. 2 line reads ‘I shall be Mr. Seek’.

find: Stevenson was writing in 1886, the year after W. T. Stead’s “Maiden Tribute” exposé
replace: Stevenson was writing in 1885, the year of W. T. Stead’s “Maiden Tribute” exposé
note: F10: Stevenson wrote the novella in 1885 and it was published on 5 January 1886; the exposé ran in July 1885.

find: Jekyll is “deadly sick”, but insists he is “done with” Hyde.
replace: Jekyll is “deathly sick”, but insists he is “done with” Hyde.
note: F11: ch. 5 reads ‘looking deathly sick’.

find: finds him transformed: “a death warrant written legibly upon his face… he had his death-warrant written there.”
replace: finds him transformed: he “had his death-warrant written legibly upon his face.”
note: F12: ch. 6 has the line once; the second half of the quotation was invented.

find: Both are men of science, but Lanyon is “hide-bound”, sticking to “the practical side of medicine”.
replace: Both are men of science, but Jekyll calls Lanyon a “hide-bound pedant”, and Lanyon holds “the most narrow and material views”.
note: F13: ‘the practical side of medicine’ is not in the novella; ‘hide-bound pedant’ is Jekyll in ch. 3 and ‘narrow and material views’ is ch. 9.

find: and newer ideas about psychology (including those of William James and early Freud) were questioning the unity of the self.
replace: and new ideas in psychology were questioning whether the mind is one thing. Freud published his theories of the unconscious later, in the 1890s, so Stevenson anticipates them rather than borrows them.
note: F14: Freud had published nothing on the unconscious in the 1880s; the novella predates him.

find: Poole, Jekyll’s butler, arrives at Utterson’s in “white and shaky” terror.
replace: Poole, Jekyll’s butler, arrives at Utterson’s in terror: “Mr Utterson, sir, I’m afraid.”
note: F15: ‘white and shaky’ is not in ch. 8; the text has ‘his face was white and his voice… harsh and broken’, later, in the square.

find: Poole notices three pieces of evidence: the voice sounds wrong, the hand glimpsed on the stair is ‘dwarfish’ and ‘hairy’, and a servant girl saw a creature ‘crying out like a rat’.
replace: Poole notices three pieces of evidence: the voice sounds wrong, the masked figure he saw himself was ‘more of a dwarf’ where his master is ‘a tall, fine build of a man’, and it cried out ‘like a rat’ and ran from him.
note: F16: in ch. 8 Poole is the witness, not a servant girl; there is no ‘dwarfish’ or ‘hairy’ hand on the stair (‘hairy’ is Jekyll’s own hand in ch. 10).

find: Jekyll’s “powers seemed shaken”, the drug stops working reliably
replace: “the powers of Hyde seemed to have grown with the sickliness of Jekyll”, the drug stops working reliably
note: F18: the quotation is invented and it reverses the sense — ch. 10 says Hyde’s powers grew as Jekyll sickened.

find: the creation of a drug that “could cast off the lower elements” of his personality.
replace: the creation of a drug that gave the “lower elements” in his soul “a second form and countenance”.
note: F19: the spliced quotation does not exist, and the drug houses the lower elements rather than casting them off.

find: I cannot, even in my own thoughts, dwell on it without a start of horror.
replace: I cannot, even in memory, dwell on it without a start of horror.
note: F20: ch. 9 reads ‘even in memory’.

find: Stevenson himself called the book ‘a fable’ — inviting interpretation.
replace: Stevenson himself called it ‘a fine bogey tale’, and he never tied it to one meaning.
note: F21: the recorded self-description is ‘a fine bogey tale’ (Lloyd Osbourne’s account of the dream). ‘A fable’ is not traced to Stevenson.

find: He is described as “lean, cold, scanty, and yet somehow lovable.”
replace: He is described as “lean, long, dusty, dreary and yet somehow lovable.”
note: F22: ch. 1 reads ‘lean, long, dusty, dreary and yet somehow lovable’.

find: The front faces a respectable square: “a certain sinister block of building” with “a great air of wealth and comfort.” But the back, facing a by-street, has a door that is “blistered and distained” with “neither bell nor knocker.”
replace: The front faces a respectable square and “wore a great air of wealth and comfort.” But the back is “a certain sinister block of building” on a by-street, with a door that is “blistered and distained” and has “neither bell nor knocker.”
note: F23: ‘a certain sinister block of building’ is the back on the by-street, not the front on the square. The lesson swapped the two faces of the house it is explaining.

find: the laboratory is described as a “dismal” former dissecting theatre.
replace: the laboratory is a “dingy, windowless structure” — a former dissecting theatre.
note: F24: ‘dismal’ describes the quarter of Soho in ch. 4; ch. 5 calls the laboratory ‘the dingy, windowless structure’.

find: When Utterson walks through London at night, “the fog settled down upon that part, as brown as umber”
replace: When Utterson rides through Soho on the first foggy morning of the season, “the fog settled down again upon that part, as brown as umber”
note: F25: ch. 4 places this at about nine in the morning, in a cab to Soho, not on a night walk.
